meta.provenance: Concepts and trap structures derived from KMF/Gremlin's GRE source set; every stem, all numbers, all options, all explanations and all figures are original. No source text or artwork reproduced. Several questions recast into numeric-entry and multiple-answer form, since the Plane Geometry source pool skews to single-answer MCQ and quantitative comparison.

questions.question: A gallery wall is covered by 48 flat rectangular panels. If each panel measures 5 feet by 4.5 feet, what is the total area, in square yards, of the panels? (Note: 1 yard = 3 feet.)
questions.explanation: Each panel covers 5 x 4.5 = 22.5 square feet, so 48 panels cover 48 x 22.5 = 1,080 square feet. Since 1 yard is 3 feet, 1 square yard is 3 x 3 = 9 square feet. Converting, 1,080/9 = 120 square yards.
questions.trap: Students divide the square-foot total by 3 instead of 9 and answer 360, or they leave the answer in square feet and choose 1,080. Converting an area between feet and yards uses the square of the length factor, so the divisor is 9.

questions.question: The figure above represents a marsh and the dry land around it. A surveyor needs the distance from point A to point B, which lie on opposite edges of the marsh and cannot be measured directly. She chooses a point R on dry land, extends line AR beyond R to a point D, and extends line BR beyond R to a point C, placing C and D so that segment CD is parallel to segment AB. She then measures RD and DC. Of the following, which additional measurement would be sufficient to determine the distance from A to B?
options: A. The distance from A to R
B. The distance from B to R
C. The distance from C to R
D. The measure of angle ARB
E. The measure of angle RAB
questions.explanation: Because CD is parallel to AB, the transversals give equal alternate interior angles, and angles DRC and ARB are vertical angles, so triangle RDC is similar to triangle RAB. Corresponding sides are then in proportion: RD/RA = DC/AB, which rearranges to AB = DC(RA)/RD. The surveyor already has DC and RD, so the one missing piece is RA, the distance from A to R. Knowing BR or CR instead would give the other proportion RC/RB = DC/AB, in which two of the three needed lengths would still be unknown, and an angle alone never fixes a length.
questions.trap: Students pick the measure of angle ARB, reasoning that an angle plus two sides determines a triangle. Angle ARB is already equal to angle DRC and so adds nothing new; similarity has already been established, and what is missing is the scale factor, which only a length along the same pair of corresponding sides can supply.

questions.question:
In triangle JKL above, the three angle bisectors meet at point N. If angle NLJ measures 21 degrees and angle NJL measures 34 degrees, what is the measure, in degrees, of angle JKN?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
questions.explanation: Since JN bisects angle J, the full angle J is 2(34) = 68 degrees. Since LN bisects angle L, the full angle L is 2(21) = 42 degrees. The three angles of triangle JKL sum to 180, so angle K = 180 - 68 - 42 = 70 degrees. KN bisects angle K, so angle JKN is half of that: 35 degrees.
questions.trap: Students find angle K = 70 and stop, choosing 70 without halving it for the bisector. Others forget to double the two given half-angles, computing 180 - 34 - 21 = 125 and then halving to 62.5. The two given angles are halves and the answer is a half, so both doublings and one halving are needed.

questions.question: The lengths of the sides of a triangle are 5, 12 and w. Which of the following inequalities specifies exactly those values of w for which every angle of the triangle measures less than 90 degrees?
questions.explanation: The angle opposite the longest side is the largest angle, and comparing the square of the longest side with the sum of the squares of the other two decides whether it is acute, right or obtuse. If w is the longest side, acuteness requires w^2 < 5^2 + 12^2 = 169, so w < 13. If 12 is the longest side, acuteness requires 12^2 < 5^2 + w^2, that is 144 < 25 + w^2, so w^2 > 119 and w > sqrt(119). Since sqrt(119) is about 10.9, which already exceeds the triangle-inequality floor of 7, the binding conditions are sqrt(119) < w < 13.
questions.trap: Students apply only the triangle inequality, 12 - 5 = 7 and 12 + 5 = 17, and pick 7 < w < 17. That range merely guarantees a triangle exists; it happily includes w = 8, where 12 is long enough to sit opposite an obtuse angle since 144 exceeds 25 + 64.

questions.question:
ABCD is a square, and AC is one of its diagonals.
Column A: (AB + BC)/AC
Column B: 1.5
options: C. The two quantities are equal
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
questions.explanation: Let the side of the square be s. Then AB = BC = s, and AC is a diagonal, which for a square equals s*sqrt(2). Column A is therefore (s + s)/(s*sqrt(2)) = 2s/(s*sqrt(2)) = 2/sqrt(2) = sqrt(2). Since sqrt(2) is about 1.414, which is less than 1.5, Column B is greater. The side length cancels, so this holds for every square.
questions.trap: Students reason that going along two sides must be much longer than cutting across, and guess a ratio near 2, choosing A. The diagonal is already sqrt(2) times a side, so two sides compared with one diagonal gives only 2/sqrt(2) = sqrt(2), which falls just short of 1.5.

questions.question:
In quadrilateral KLMN above, side LM is parallel to side KN, LM is shorter than KN, and angle K is a right angle.

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
Column A: The length of KL
Column B: The length of MN
questions.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 220" width="320" height="220" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><g stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="2"><polygon points="50,190 50,60 170,60 270,190"/><polyline points="50,178 62,178 62,190"/></g><g font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937"><text x="36" y="206">K</text><text x="36" y="56">L</text><text x="172" y="52">M</text><text x="276" y="206">N</text></g></svg>
options: C. The two quantities are equal
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
questions.explanation: Because angle K is a right angle and LM is parallel to KN, side KL is perpendicular to both parallel lines, so KL is exactly the perpendicular distance between them. Now drop a perpendicular from M to line KN, meeting it at a point F. Then MF also equals that same distance, so MF = KL. Since LM is shorter than KN, the point F falls strictly between K and N, so FN is a positive length and triangle MFN is a genuine right triangle with legs MF and FN and hypotenuse MN. A hypotenuse always exceeds either leg, so MN is greater than MF = KL.
questions.trap: Students see no numbers and choose 'cannot be determined'. The perpendicular side KL is the shortest possible segment between the two parallel lines, and because LM is strictly shorter than KN the side MN must slant, which forces it to be strictly longer, whatever the actual measurements are.

questions.question:
O is a point in a plane, and X, Y and Z are three distinct points in that same plane with OX = OY = OZ = 9.
Column A: XY
Column B: YZ
options: C. The two quantities are equal
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
questions.explanation: Saying that X, Y and Z are all 9 units from O places all three on one circle of radius 9 centred at O, but it says nothing about where on that circle they sit. The length XY depends only on the central angle XOY, and YZ only on the central angle YOZ, and those two angles are completely free. For instance, putting X, Y and Z at 0, 60 and 180 degrees around the circle makes XY = 9 and YZ = 9*sqrt(3), so Column B wins; swapping the roles of X and Z makes Column A win. Nothing decides between them.
questions.trap: Students read three equal distances from one point as forcing an equilateral triangle and answer 'equal'. Equal distances from O only put the three points on a common circle; the chords between them still vary with how the points are spaced around it.

questions.question:
In triangle ABC above, angle A is a right angle, AB = 20 and AC = 48. Point D lies on side AC with AD = (5/12)(AC). What is the measure, in degrees, of angle BDC?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
questions.explanation: First locate D: AD = (5/12)(48) = 20. So in triangle ABD the two legs at the right angle A are AB = 20 and AD = 20, making it an isosceles right triangle. Its two acute angles are therefore 45 degrees each, so angle ADB = 45. Since D lies on segment AC, angles ADB and BDC together form a straight angle, so angle BDC = 180 - 45 = 135 degrees.
questions.trap: Students compute angle ADB = 45 and submit that, answering the wrong angle. Angle BDC is the one on the far side of D, the supplement of angle ADB, so it is obtuse at 135 degrees.

questions.question: A 25-foot ladder leans against a vertical wall with the base of the ladder 7 feet from the wall. The base is then pulled 8 feet farther from the wall, and the top of the ladder slides down the wall. By how many feet does the top of the ladder drop?
questions.explanation: The ladder, the wall and the ground form a right triangle with the ladder as the 25-foot hypotenuse. At first the base is 7 feet out, so the top reaches sqrt(625 - 49) = sqrt(576) = 24 feet up the wall. After the base is pulled out 8 more feet it sits 15 feet from the wall, so the top now reaches sqrt(625 - 225) = sqrt(400) = 20 feet. The top therefore drops 24 - 20 = 4 feet.
questions.trap: Students assume the top falls as far as the base moves and answer 8. The two distances are linked by the Pythagorean theorem, not by a one-to-one trade: near the vertical position the top barely moves, so an 8-foot pull out costs only 4 feet of height here.

questions.question:
In the figure above, ACEG is a square. Square ABIH shares vertex A with it, with B on side AC and H on side AG. Square JDEF shares vertex E with it, with D on side CE and F on side EG. Squares ABIH and JDEF have equal areas, and the area of square ACEG is 25 times the area of square ABIH. BJFI is a parallelogram. If the area of square ABIH is 20, what is the area of parallelogram BJFI?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
questions.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 300 260" width="300" height="260" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><polygon points="40,180 200,60 240,60 80,180" fill="#e5edf7" stroke="none"/><g stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="2"><rect x="40" y="20" width="200" height="200"/><rect x="40" y="180" width="40" height="40"/><rect x="200" y="20" width="40" height="40"/><polygon points="40,180 200,60 240,60 80,180"/></g><g font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937"><text x="26" y="234">A</text><text x="24" y="186">B</text><text x="26" y="16">C</text><text x="192" y="14">D</text><text x="244" y="16">E</text><text x="246" y="64">F</text><text x="244" y="234">G</text><text x="74" y="236">H</text><text x="87" y="197">I</text><text x="185" y="48">J</text></g></svg>
questions.explanation: Let each small square have side s, so its area is s^2 = 20. Since square ACEG has 25 times that area, its side is 5s. Put A at the origin with AG along one axis and AC along the other. Then B is s from A along AC and I is the far corner of the small square, so segment BI is horizontal with length s and sits s from side AG. The far small square at E puts J and F at a height of 5s - s = 4s, with JF horizontal of length s. So BJFI has base BI = s and its opposite side JF parallel to it at a height of 4s - s = 3s. Its area is base times height = s(3s) = 3s^2 = 3(20) = 60.
questions.trap: Students take the parallelogram's height to be the full 4s that separates the two small squares' far edges and answer 80, or they slide the slanted side BJ into the area formula and use it as a height. The height of a parallelogram is the perpendicular distance between the two parallel sides BI and JF, which is 3s, not 4s and not the slant.

questions.question:
The distance from the centre of tree P to the centre of tree Q is 30 feet, and the distance from the centre of tree P to the centre of tree R is 18 feet. The centres of the three trees are not in a straight line. Which of the following could be the distance, in feet, from the centre of tree Q to the centre of tree R?

Indicate all such values.
questions.explanation: The three centres form a triangle, so QR must be greater than the difference of the other two sides and less than their sum: 30 - 18 = 12 and 30 + 18 = 48, giving 12 < QR < 48. Of the choices, 20, 36 and 45 lie strictly inside. 10 is below the range, and 12 and 48 are the excluded endpoints.
questions.trap: Students include 12 or 48, the two boundary values. Each of those would place the three centres on a single line, which the problem explicitly rules out, so both bounds are open.

questions.question:
Square WXYZ and parallelogram WPQZ lie in the same plane and share the side WZ. Also, WP = WX, points P and X lie on the same side of line WZ, and P is not the same point as X. Which of the following must be true?

Indicate all such statements.
options: A. The area of WXYZ is greater than the area of WPQZ
B. The perimeter of WXYZ is equal to the perimeter of WPQZ
D. The area of WPQZ is greater than half the area of WXYZ
E. The area of WXYZ is more than twice the area of WPQZ
questions.explanation: Let the shared side WZ have length a. The square has all four sides equal to a. Since WP = WX = a, the parallelogram has WP = a as well, and in a parallelogram opposite sides are equal, so PQ = WZ = a and ZQ = WP = a. That settles two statements at once: PQ = a = XY, so C is true, and both figures have perimeter 4a, so B is true. For areas, both figures sit on base WZ = a. The square's height is the full a, because WX is perpendicular to WZ. The parallelogram's height is a times the sine of angle PWZ. Because P and X lie on the same side of line WZ with WP = WX = a, both P and X sit on the same semicircle of radius a centred at W, so P not equal to X forces angle PWZ to differ from angle XWZ = 90 degrees. The sine is then strictly less than 1 and the parallelogram's area is strictly less than a^2. So A is true. But nothing pins down how far the parallelogram leans: the angle could be near 90 degrees, making its area almost a^2, or very small, making its area nearly zero. So D and E can each fail, and the parallelogram's diagonal WQ likewise varies with the lean while WY is fixed at a*sqrt(2), so F can fail.
questions.trap: Students reject B, assuming a leaning shape must have a different perimeter from the square. Tilting the square into a rhombus keeps every side at length a, so the perimeter is untouched; it is the area, which depends on the height, that shrinks.
